title: Travelling with a drone
body:
O.P.
Hi all,
I have a DJI Mavic 4 Pro drone with a hard case.
Have you/would you travel with a drone? Has it added to your experience or did you find it an unnecessary extra that you had to carry around with minimal benefit?
A friend of mine travels with hers and swears by it, but I'm inclined to think that it would be more of a burden than anything although I can see how it would be beneficial to get a 'feel' of your surroundings in particular awesome landscapes etc.
Have you done this and what are your thoughts?

---- replies ----
[User #1917620765 postsVandelay IndustriesAll your base are belong to usWhirlpool Forums Addict] Bit Of Dis'N Dat writes...
Have you done this and what are your thoughts?
Definitely brush up on the drone laws of the country you are visiting. It can vary a lot by jurisdiction.
In saying that, there are some places in the world where a skilled drone operator could get some amazing footage
[User #9276410387 postsfriesianWhirlpool Forums Addict] Bit Of Dis'N Dat writes...
I have a DJI Mavic 4 Pro drone
Bit big to carry around travelling, don't you think? Get something smaller if you just want to document your holidays.
I watch a travel couple of YouTube who seem to have a lot of drone shots of the places they visit. https://www.youtube.com/@SammyandTommy
[User #4363143945 postsTomColeWhirlpool Forums Addict] Steve is a tourist bus driver and says that most of his passengers are nice and polite but occasionally he gets an ill-mannered loud mouth job like Brad. Bus stopped at a noted beauty spot within a National Park; Steve explained a little about local flora and fauna and suggested his passengers consider walking around the lake – about 40 minutes.
"No need" says Brad : "I will just sit here and send my drone." And he did. The drone then crashed.
Steve was asked to go and retrieve the drone several hundred metres away. Steve declined as for safety and security reasons and company policy he had to stay close to the bus. Then along comes a Parks Ranger in uniform, a lowly public servant. According to Steve, passenger Brad basically ordered the Ranger to go and retrieve his drone. "Are you saying, Sir, that that yellow thing up on that ridge is your drone?" "Yes, Sir." "Well you had better go and get it or else I will have to book you for littering in a National Park, and confiscate the drone as evidence."
An unexpected complication from having a drone.
[Names have not been changed to protect the guilty.]

[User #90105334 postsBit Of Dis'N  DatParticipant] O.P.
Vandelay Industries writes...
Definitely brush up on the drone laws of the country you are visiting. It can vary a lot by jurisdiction.
Yeah from what I've read, Europe is probably the most restrictive. However, I don't think Europe would be a great location to fly a drone anyway. Too congested and more likely to upset the locals. I was thinking New Zealand and the US (outside the metro areas) where you can appreciate the vast open landscape.
I'll have to read up on all the regulations but I was surprised by the US seemingly lax restrictions on night time flying.. but then Australia has always been excessive when it comes to laws and regulation. The red tape and financial overheads just to get a drone license is absurd. One only needs to look at CASA's sudden 'temporary' lift of the drone ban over Cronulla the day after the shark attack to realise this. No plane ever flies near 120m (the maximum allowed drone height) that far from the runway. It was purely overreach. That said, at least for recreational pilots at least you don't need to register the drone (yet).
friesian writes...
Bit big to carry around travelling, don't you think? Get something smaller if you just want to document your holidays.
Agreed, it's not the easiest thing to haul around. But even the smaller drones like Avata 2 (which I crashed into the river!!) are still an effort by the time you include cables, batteries & accessories etc. Plus with the extra size you get much better footage and ability to zoom from afar.
TomCole writes...
Steve is a tourist bus driver
I've used Whirlpool quite a lot over the years but hands down that would have to be the lamest, pointless post ever. I can only assume there was a valid point you were making and I missed it entirely. But thanks for the effort :-D
[User #336472158 postsBSArtisti am a happy mushroomWhirlpool Forums Addict] Bit Of Dis'N Dat writes...
Have you done this and what are your thoughts?
Speaking from a personal view.... Yes I bring my DJI Neo along on some trips. Yes it is a mix bag feeling.
Got some footage on Fraser Island, some footage from WA south west. No footage from Tassie as it was banned in Nat Park (should have checked else I won't bother bringing).
Is it worth the trouble? Maybe not. Mostly not. Not for the few clips that I got anyway. Being fragile I had to take it along as hand carry. Mostly I tried to travel light with a single cabin bag, with both drone + controller + batteries pack, does not leave much room/ weight for anything else.
But if I am having a road trip, I will definately bring it along ;-) much easier in the car
[User #1763818229 postsTicTacToetrained chickenWhirlpool Forums Addict] Bit Of Dis'N Dat writes...
I was thinking New Zealand and the US (outside the metro areas) where you can appreciate the vast open landscape.
The US is probably one of the least restrictive but you still can't (legally) do US National Parks and most (but not all) State Parks.
In Canada pretty much anywhere there are tourists, there are drone bans. I suspect NZ is going to be closer to that than the US situation.
[User #336472158 postsBSArtisti am a happy mushroomWhirlpool Forums Addict] Gone are the good old days of carefree drone flying anywhere :-D Whats the point of having a drone when you can't legally fly them in the most scenic spots in the world *shruck*
The most surprising is that I think China is the most easy to fly drone. Just have to register your drone at the local police station and off you go.
Obviously you can't / shouldn't fly in cities with dense population. You don't want to injure someone if the drone falls out of the sky.
[User #4363143945 postsTomColeWhirlpool Forums Addict] BSArtist writes...
Gone are the good old days of carefree drone flying anywhere
So true.
I live in inner city and kids often fly drones in the local dog park, fine, but if a drone strays across the road into the wharf zone then the stasi are alerted.
The kids love the park. Good grass, slight slope so excellent visibility, the braver or more experienced can test their skills flying between branches of mature trees, and the dogs love chasing a drone flying at about a metre. When drone lands dogs instantly lose interest. Quite a sight – a dozen dogs bounding behind a drone.
[User #2699617629 postsEwen HoosarmiWhirlpool Forums Addict] BSArtist writes...
Whats the point of having a drone when you can't legally fly them in the most scenic spots in the world
It begs the question – why are sight seeing helicopters exempt from flying bans in NPs when the reasons why we can't fly drones is that it'll upset the native fauna?
A chopper is a tad louder, a tad bigger and flies a lot faster than a drone.
[User #4131551524 postsdellvostroWhirlpool Enthusiast] Helicopters are banned in 90% of national parks in the USA. In the few places where they are permitted, the designated flight paths are designed firstly for safety, then to avoid bothering native fauna and other park visitors.
[User #742437049 postsTheDocWhirlpool Forums Addict] Ewen Hoosarmi writes...
It begs the question – why are sight seeing helicopters exempt from flying bans in NPs when the reasons why we can't fly drones is that it'll upset the native fauna?
Helicopters are generally not allowed fly below 500 feet over most areas, and in many parks there are Fly Neighbourly Advice's that restrict them to above 1000-1500 feet (technically an FNA is voluntary, but they are still generally honored). Drones obviously operate much lower than that – and in most cases would be starting at 0 feet above ground.
In much of the US, there's technically a loophole to the regulations that the parks can't stop you flying a drone above the park (in the same way a helicopter would), they can only stop you taking off/landing in a park. So you can technically take off outside of the park and fly into it, then exit it again before landing.
dellvostro writes...
Helicopters are banned in 90% of national parks in the USA.
Not quite. They are allowed to fly over most US National Park, but must maintain at least 2000 ft above ground level. There are further restrictions in some parks (eg, Yosemite, where you can be 2000 ft above ground level, and still 1000+ ft below the top of the cliff next to you!)
